CausalChain: Oncogenic miRNAs (e.g., miR-155) are selectively loaded into exosomes via sumoylated hnRNPA2B1 -> Exosomes transfer these miRNAs to adjacent cancer cells -> Delivered miR-155 suppresses tumor suppressor targets (e.g., TP53INP1, GATA3), promoting EMT -> EMT fosters acquisition of stem-like properties and drug resistance -> Inhibition of hnRNPA2B1 sumoylation reduces exosomal miR-155 delivery -> Reduced EMT leads to increased chemosensitivity
Hypothesis: Inhibition of hnRNPA2B1 sumoylation disrupts the exosomal loading and intercellular transfer of oncogenic miRNAs (such as miR-155), thereby reducing EMT induction and reversing chemoresistance in cancer cells.
Abstract: Recent studies have implicated exosome‐mediated transfer of microRNAs in the induction of epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and subsequent drug resistance across several cancer types. In our hypothesis, we propose that the sumoylation of the RNA‐binding protein hnRNPA2B1—which has been shown to control the selective loading of miRNAs into exosomes—plays a critical role in the paracrine spread of oncogenic miRNAs such as miR‐155. Disruption of hnRNPA2B1 sumoylation is expected to reduce the exosomal cargo of these EMT‐promoting miRNAs, thereby limiting intercellular signaling that leads to EMT and chemoresistance. This approach represents a potential novel strategy to re‐sensitize cancer cells to chemotherapeutic agents by mitigating EMT-driven drug resistance.
